la:adj:Pompeius.html:
Pompējus (trisyl.) or Pompēïus (quadrisyl.), i, m., and Pompēja, ae, f.,
name of a Roman gens. So the famous Cn. Pompejus Magnus, the triumvir, ; ; ; sqq. et saep.—In fem., Pompeja, his sister, ; another,his daughter,; a third,daughter of Q. Pompeius, wife of Julius Cœsar, divorced from him,; .— Hence,
Pompējus (Pompēïus), a, um, adj., of or belonging to a Pompey, Pompeian: domus,: lex,: porticus,at Rome, (3, 30, 11); cf. ; : via,leading through Sicily,: ficus,.—
Pompējānus, a, um, adj., of Pompey, Pompeian: equitatus,: classis,: triumphi,: caedes,: porticus (usually called Pompeja porticus),: theatrum,; ; hence also, Notus,which blew in Pompey's theatre,: ficus (also called Pompeja ficus), Cloat. ap. : partes,.—
Subst.: Pompējāni, ōrum, m., the adherents or soldiers of Pompey, Pompey's party, Pompey's troops, ; ; .—In sing., : Pompejanus Cilix,.

la:noun:pompa.html:
pompa, ae, f., = πομπή,
a solemn procession,a public procession of any kind (at public festivals, games, triumphs, marriages, funerals, etc.).
Lit.
In gen.: in pompā cum magna vis auri argentique ferretur,: per Dionysia pompam ducere,: sollemnes ordine pompas Exequi,: sollemnes ducere pompas Ad delubra juvat,: Pontico triumpho inter pompae fercula trium verborum protulit titulum: veni, vidi, vici,; so, pompa Indica,i. e. the triumphal procession of Bacchus,: cadaver Clodii spoliatum exsequiis, pompā,; so of a funeral procession, ; cf.: pompam funeris ire,to attend a funeral,: pompam parare triumphis,: exornaturus victoris superbi pompam,: pomparum ferculis similes esse (referring to the slowness of such processions),.—
In partic., the processions at the Circensian games, in which images of the gods were carried, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; so of Cæsar, whose image was carried among them: tu hunc de pompā, Quirini contubernalem, laetaturum putas?.—
Transf.
A train, suite, retinue, row, array of persons or things (class.), ; : molesta haec pompa lictorum meorum,: postremo tota petitio cura ut pompae plena sit,: captivorum,.—Of things: pecuniae pompa,: ventri portatur pompa, i. e. rich repast, Plaut. Fragm. ap. : munera certā discurrunt pompā,: sarcinarum,: strepitus pompae armorum,.—
Parade, display, ostentation, pomp (class.; syn. apparatus): rhetorum pompa,: in dicendo adhibere quandam speciem atque pompam,: detraxit muneri suo pompam,: ad pompam vel ostentationem aliquid accipere,: genus orationis pompae quam pugnae aptius,; so, eorum partim in pompā, partim in acie illustres esse voluerunt,.

senses: to act pompously (with pomp)

pompo, no

la:noun:pomerium.html:
pōmērĭum and pōmoerĭum (the first is most freq. in inscrr., the latter in MSS.;
but the better manuscripts have also,, and and 24, pomerium. A third form, post-moerium, Müll., seems merely to have been assumed from the etymology; a fourth archaic form is posi-merium, pontificale pomoerium, qui auspicato olim quidem omnem urbem ambiebat praeter Aventinum ... estque prosimerium quasi proxi-murium, pontifices auspicabantur, Paul. ex Müll.), ĭi, n.
post-moerus = murus
.
Lit., the open space left free from buildings within and without the walls of a town, bounded by stones (cippi or termini), and limiting the city auspices, Müll.; ; ; ; and 24: POMERIVM, Inscr. (746 A. U. C.) Orell. 1; (Orell. 1, p. 567); ; Inscr. (A. D. 121) Orell. 811: pomoerium intrare, transire,: de pomoerii jure,: sales intra pomeria nati,i. e. of the city,.—
Trop., bounds, limits (ante- and post-class.): qui minore pomerio finierunt,who have prescribed narrower limits to themselves,; .
